geographic_scope: Statewide commercial UAS operations for which federal certification is required
issuing_authority: Utah Legislature and Utah Department of Transportation
source_title: Commercial UAS state registration and UDOT pre-registration process
citation: Utah Code §§ 72-10-109(4), 72-10-110(4); UDOT Aircraft Registration — Drone Registration
status: Current / in force; official portal pending
binding_level: Binding statute and official agency procedure
uas_topic: State registration; annual certificate; fee rule; pre-registration
regulated_party: Commercial UAS operators and owners whose operation requires federal certification
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS commercially in Utah and obtaining the state operating certificate
requirement_type: State registration requirement administered through interim pre-registration
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — current UDOT pre-registration, followed by fee payment and certificate through the announced portal
summary: Beginning January 1, 2025, Utah Code § 72-10-109 prohibits commercial operation in Utah of a UAS for which federal certification is required unless the aircraft has a current Utah Department of Transportation registration certificate. Section 72-10-110 directs UDOT to establish UAS registration fees and related rules. UDOT states that commercial and government operators should currently submit its pre-registration form while the official portal is developed, with launch expected in late summer 2026, and that pre-registration complies with state code until operators are contacted to pay and obtain a state operating certificate.
verification_status: Verified against current Utah Code and current UDOT registration page

geographic_scope: Political subdivisions statewide, with airport-operator exceptions
source_title: Preemption of local UAS ordinances and statewide recognition of business licenses
uas_topic: State preemption; airport authority; local business licensing
regulated_party: Political subdivisions, airport operators, and Part 107 or Part 135 commercial UAS businesses
regulated_activity: Local regulation of private UAS use and licensing of commercial UAS businesses
requirement_type: State preemption with airport exception and single-license recognition framework
permit_or_approval_required: A political subdivision may require one business license only when the business lacks a current license in good standing from another Utah subdivision
summary: Section 72-10-701 generally bars Utah political subdivisions from regulating private UAS use unless Chapter 10 authorizes the rule or an airport operator governs operations within airport boundaries or takeoff and landing at its airport. A commercial Part 107 or Part 135 UAS business may be required to obtain one local business license if it lacks a current license in good standing elsewhere in Utah, but other subdivisions must recognize that license. Fees are limited to actual processing cost, and multiple subdivision licenses or per-employee licenses are prohibited.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Utah Code page
notes: The statute supersedes political-subdivision UAS laws enacted before July 1, 2022. Local ordinance research is deferred under project scope.

geographic_scope: Statewide law-enforcement acquisition, receipt, and use of UAS data
uas_topic: Law enforcement; warrants; nongovernment data; emergency; surveillance
regulated_party: Law-enforcement agencies and officers; nongovernment data sources
regulated_activity: Obtaining, receiving, using, and destroying data acquired through UAS or associated imaging devices
requirement_type: Use restriction with warrant, exception, emergency, and privacy pathways
permit_or_approval_required: A warrant or recognized exception may be required depending on purpose and privacy expectations
public_agency_only: Yes, but expressly addresses data obtained from nongovernment actors
commercial_operator_relevance: High for law-enforcement clients or requested data transfers
summary: Section 72-10-802 prohibits a law-enforcement agency or officer from obtaining, receiving, or using UAS-acquired data unless it is obtained under a warrant, a judicially recognized warrant exception, qualifying circumstances involving a nongovernment actor, a lost-person search where no reasonable expectation of privacy exists, or another method that does not violate a reasonable expectation of privacy. Nongovernment data may be used for law-enforcement purposes only when it appears crime-related or supports a good-faith imminent or ongoing emergency. Covered data must be destroyed as soon as reasonably possible, subject to applicable retention law.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Utah Code page effective May 6, 2026
notes: The section applies to an imaging surveillance device used with a UAS. It can affect a consultant asked to provide imagery or data to law enforcement.

geographic_scope: Statewide law-enforcement data involving persons, structures, or areas outside a mission target
source_title: Law-enforcement UAS data retention and incidental collection
uas_topic: Data retention; incidental collection; disclosure; public lands
regulated_activity: Using, copying, disclosing, and destroying nontarget UAS data
requirement_type: Data minimization and destruction requirement with enumerated exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: No operator application stated; court orders and statutory exceptions can alter retention
commercial_operator_relevance: Moderate for law-enforcement clients and data processors
summary: Section 72-10-803 generally bars a law-enforcement agency from using, copying, or disclosing UAS data about a person, structure, or area that was not a mission target and requires destruction as soon as reasonably possible under applicable law. Exceptions cover inseparable target data, court-ordered or nongovernment-actor data, inadvertent collection that appears crime-related, emergency information whose use or disclosure would assist the response, and data collected over public lands outside municipal boundaries. The duty applies to the agency, but a contractor handling agency data may need to support the agency's retention and deletion controls.
verification_status: Verified against the current official Utah Code section PDF and current chapter text
notes: This record is separated from § 72-10-802 because it addresses nontarget retention rather than the initial legal basis for acquisition or use.

source_title: Weapon attached to an unmanned aircraft
revision_date: Definitions amended in 2025; current code reviewed 2026-08-02
uas_topic: Weaponized UAS; payload; federal approval; government contract
regulated_party: Any person operating a UAS carrying or fitted with a weapon
regulated_activity: Flying a UAS that carries a weapon or has a weapon attached
requirement_type: Criminal prohibition with federal-approval, government-contract, and DOD-airspace exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: FAA written approval, an authorizing state or federal contract, or DOD permission is required for the corresponding exception
commercial_operator_relevance: Moderate for unusual payloads and government work
summary: Section 72-10-902 makes flying an unmanned aircraft that carries or has an attached weapon a class B misdemeanor. The statutory weapon definition includes a firearm and an object capable, in its use or intended use, of causing death, bodily injury, or property damage under listed contextual factors. Exceptions apply when the operator follows an FAA certificate of authorization or other written approval, performs under a state or federal contract that permits the armed operation, or operates with Department of Defense permission in DOD-controlled airspace.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Utah Code page and current chapter text
notes: The contextual weapon definition warrants review of unusual release, impact, or mitigation payloads; ordinary sensing payloads are not identified as weapons.

geographic_scope: Property of a correctional facility statewide
source_title: Unlawful operation of a UAS near a correctional facility
uas_topic: Corrections; item delivery or removal; facility security
regulated_party: Any UAS operator, with a mosquito-abatement employee or contractor exception
regulated_activity: Carrying, dropping, or removing items at correctional property or interfering with facility operations or security
requirement_type: Criminal prohibition with narrow employment exception
summary: Section 72-10-903 prohibits operating a UAS to carry or drop any item to or inside correctional-facility property, to remove any item from inside that property, or to interfere with facility operations or security. Carrying, dropping, or removing an item is a third-degree felony; operational or security interference is a class B misdemeanor. The 2026 amendment preserves a narrow exception for an employee or contractor working for a mosquito-abatement district while acting within the scope of employment. The text does not publish a general consultant permit or consent exception.
verification_status: Verified against enrolled 2026 SB 93 and current official Utah Code chapter text
notes: The offense concerns specified conduct at correctional property rather than a stated fixed-distance buffer. Facility and property authorization remain separate mission-planning questions.

source_title: Safe UAS operation — visual line of sight, airspace, airport, notice, and altitude rules
uas_topic: Visual line of sight; controlled airspace; airports; notices to airmen; altitude; penalties
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS in Utah airspace
requirement_type: Operating restrictions with civil liability and escalating enforcement
permit_or_approval_required: Air-traffic-control authorization and FAA altitude waivers apply where specified
summary: Section 72-10-1002 requires an individual operator to maintain visual line of sight directly or through a visual observer, obtain air-traffic-control authorization for listed controlled airspace, avoid interfering with airports, heliports, or seaplane bases, comply with the cited notice-to-airmen rule, and remain at or below 400 feet unless the stated structure exception or an FAA waiver applies. Violations can create civil liability. Enforcement begins with a written warning, then escalates to an infraction and, after prior convictions, a class B misdemeanor.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Utah Code page
notes: Some provisions track federal operating concepts but are independently stated in Utah law. This record does not replace live airspace review.

geographic_scope: Public-transit rail property and surface critical-infrastructure facilities statewide
source_title: Safe UAS operation — public transit and critical infrastructure
uas_topic: Public transit; rail; critical infrastructure; facility authorization
regulated_party: Individuals operating unmanned aircraft, including contractors
regulated_activity: Launching from transit facilities, low operations over guideways and electric lines, and overflight of surface critical infrastructure
requirement_type: Location-based prohibition with client, law-enforcement, and regulatory-agency exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: Prior facility authorization is required for ordinary operation over surface critical infrastructure
summary: Section 72-10-1002 prohibits ordinary UAS operation from a public-transit rail platform or station and specified flight below 50 feet within a fixed-guideway right-of-way directly over traction-power lines. An employee or contractor of a large public transit district may use a UAS there for listed safety purposes. The section separately bars operation over a defined surface critical-infrastructure facility without prior facility authorization, except for first responders and state or federal regulators. A consultant's client relationship alone does not appear to create the regulatory-agency exception.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Utah Code page
notes: Surface critical infrastructure is defined in Utah Code § 76-6-106.3. Obtain the facility owner or operator's written authorization for ordinary consultant operations.

geographic_scope: Public-entity critical-infrastructure inspections and contractors working directly for public entities
source_title: Covered-foreign-entity UAS restriction for public critical-infrastructure inspection
uas_topic: Procurement; covered foreign entity; cybersecurity; critical infrastructure; public contracts
regulated_party: Public entities and contractors working directly for public entities
regulated_activity: Purchasing or operating UAS for critical-infrastructure inspection
permit_or_approval_required: No state application stated; the public entity must ensure the statutory controls
public_agency_only: No — expressly reaches direct public-entity contractors
summary: Sections 72-10-1201 and 1202 prohibit a public entity or a contractor working directly for one from purchasing or operating, for critical-infrastructure inspection, a UAS manufactured or assembled by a covered foreign entity. Regardless of origin, an otherwise covered UAS may be operated when the public entity ensures it remains disconnected from the Internet during inspection, all collected imagery, geospatial data, and flight logs are removed before later Internet connection, and any required Internet video broadcast uses U.S.-developed software or software approved under the latest National Defense Authorization Act.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Utah Code page and statutory definitions
notes: The rule is mission- and client-specific rather than a statewide ban on owning a listed manufacturer's aircraft. Contract documents may impose stricter flow-down terms.

source_title: Unlawful privacy violation and UAS commercial-purpose defense
uas_topic: Privacy; surveillance; commercial defense; ground-penetrating technology; surveying
regulated_party: Persons using surveillance devices or ground-penetrating technology, including UAS operators
regulated_activity: Observing or recording events in a private place and collecting protected subsurface property data
requirement_type: Criminal and civil privacy prohibition with UAS and land-surveyor defenses
permit_or_approval_required: Consent may be required; no agency permit stated
summary: Section 76-12-302 makes specified unauthorized surveillance of a private place, and certain nonconsensual ground-penetrating collection about property, a class B misdemeanor with possible destruction of data and civil remedies. A UAS operator has a defense when the flight serves a legitimate commercial or educational purpose, follows applicable FAA authority, and any otherwise prohibited conduct is solely incidental to that lawful use. A land surveyor performing a bona fide contract receives a separate ground-penetrating-data exception only if irrelevant data about noncontract property is not distributed and is destroyed after the contract.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Utah Code page
notes: The commercial UAS provision is a defense with factual elements, not blanket immunity. Ground-penetrating obligations are relevant only when that technology is actually used.

uas_topic: Trespass; private property; notice; intent; fear; civil damages
regulated_party: Persons causing an unmanned aircraft to enter or remain over private property
regulated_activity: Unlawful UAS presence over private property with specified intent, recklessness, or notice
permit_or_approval_required: Property authorization defeats the UAS-specific remain-unlawfully element; no agency permit stated
summary: Section 76-6-206 defines entry to include an entire unmanned aircraft and treats a UAS as remaining unlawfully over private property when the property is not open to the public and the operator lacks authorization. Criminal trespass requires additional statutory circumstances, including intent to annoy, injure, damage property, or commit a specified crime; recklessness about causing fear; or knowing unlawful presence after legally sufficient notice. Penalties vary by conduct, and the statute authorizes statutory damages, attorney fees, and costs. Authorized or public access under lawful conditions provides a stated defense.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Utah Code page
notes: Unauthorized overflight alone is not summarized as automatically satisfying every offense element; intent, recklessness, or notice requirements remain material.

geographic_scope: FAA wildfire temporary flight restrictions and government-designated wildland-fire scenes
uas_topic: Wildfire; temporary flight restriction; incident commander; emergency response; neutralization
regulated_party: UAS operators, sanctioned entities, incident commanders, and law enforcement
regulated_activity: Operating within a wildfire TFR or officially designated wildland-fire scene
requirement_type: Operational prohibition with incident-command permission pathway, penalties, and neutralization authority
permit_or_approval_required: Incident-commander permission and compliance with imposed restrictions are required
summary: Section 65A-3-2.5 prohibits UAS flight within an FAA wildfire temporary flight restriction or an area officially designated as a wildland-fire scene unless the incident commander grants permission and the operator follows imposed restrictions. Reckless violations carry escalating misdemeanor or felony penalties based on interference, contact, or crash consequences, plus possible restitution. The incident commander must grant reasonable, safely conditioned access within three miles to listed sanctioned entities, which include utilities, pipeline operators, insurers, resource-extraction entities, news media, and certain FAA-authorized operators. Officials may neutralize a violating aircraft when reasonably necessary.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current Utah Code page
notes: AEC consultants are not automatically sanctioned entities, but may qualify when working under the direction of a listed entity or under express FAA authority described by the statute.

source_title: Harassment of livestock using a UAS
regulated_party: Any UAS operator, subject to owner, agent, emergency, government, and husbandry exceptions
regulated_activity: Intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly chasing or harming livestock with a UAS
requirement_type: Criminal prohibition with stated exceptions and escalating penalties
permit_or_approval_required: No agency permit stated; owner direction or permission is a statutory exception
commercial_operator_relevance: High for rural, agricultural, and corridor work
summary: Section 76-13-214 prohibits intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly chasing livestock with intent to cause distress, or harming livestock, through use of a UAS. A qualifying violation is generally a class B misdemeanor but becomes a class A misdemeanor for a repeat offense, serious injury or death, or livestock or property damage over $1,000 including recovery cost. Exceptions cover the livestock owner, an employee or agent acting with owner direction or permission, emergency action to protect livestock or property, government personnel acting officially, and generally accepted animal-husbandry practices.
verification_status: Verified against the current official Utah Code section PDF and part index
notes: AEC missions should maintain separation and adapt flight profiles when livestock show distress; owner permission is material but does not waive unrelated safety rules.

source_title: Commercial and drone use permits on state-park property
citation: Utah Admin. Code R651-601-16, R651-635-1 to -5; official park drone and Special Use Permit pages
effective_date: April 25, 2023 rule update; current park pages reviewed 2026-08-02
status: Current / in force; park-specific conditions vary
binding_level: Binding property-use rule and official permit requirements
uas_topic: State parks; commercial activity; Special Use Permit; drone permission; insurance; seasonal restrictions
regulated_party: Commercial operators and other persons using UAS from state-park property
regulated_activity: Commercial activity and park-specific drone launch, landing, and operation
requirement_type: Advance discretionary permit and park-specific operating conditions
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — commercial activity requires a permit; park pages commonly require a Special Use Permit and separate drone permission
summary: Utah Administrative Code defines unmanned aircraft and generally requires a permit before commercial, privileged, or special use on Division-managed park property. Requests ordinarily go to the local park manager, region, or main office at least 30 business days before the proposed activity; approval is discretionary and liability insurance may be required. Official park pages add location-specific drone conditions. Examples include commercial Special Use Permits, separate drone forms, seasonal or area closures, launch-site limits, fees, proof of a remote-pilot certificate, and longer local lead times. The precise park's current instructions control the property-use process.

notes: The source URL is an official example that distinguishes personal drone permission from commercial Special Use Permits. Confirm the specific park because conditions are not uniform.

source_title: Commission of an offense with the aid of an unmanned aircraft
uas_topic: Criminal responsibility; use of UAS to aid an offense
regulated_party: Any actor controlling a UAS while committing an offense
regulated_activity: Committing another offense with the aid of an unmanned aircraft
summary: Section 76-2-106 provides that an actor may be found guilty of an offense when the actor commits that offense with the aid of an unmanned aircraft and the associated UAS is under the actor's control at the time. The section uses the UAS definitions in Utah Code § 72-10-102. It does not create a standalone operating permit or identify a separate offense level; instead, it establishes how controlled UAS use can support criminal responsibility for another underlying offense, such as conduct addressed by Utah's trespass, privacy, or interference provisions.
verification_status: Verified against current Utah Code structure and official enacted/codified text
notes: This provision is included because it expressly applies general criminal responsibility to UAS-assisted conduct; it should not be read as criminalizing ordinary lawful commercial use.
